Are we interpreting the model of interest?

Are we interpreting the model of interest?

TL;DR: The same model checkpoint can behave differently under different attention implementations or floating-point precisions. If inspecting a model changes its execution, are we still interpreting the computation that produced the behavior of interest? I look into the problem of attention extraction specifically in this blog and show how to recover attention patterns from an opaque attention backend while preserving downstream computation.

2026-11-11 · Etha Tianze Hua · GitHub Repo
ContentsPart 0: Getting attention weights can make a model behave differentlyPart I: Same weights can produce different behavioral outputs under different attention implementationsPart II: Recovering attention from fused kernelsRelated issues reported onlineDiscussionAppendix: eager generation across precisionsAppendix: five more images with different continuationsAppendix: five more prefixes with different continuations

The model we interpret should be the same computational artifact that exhibits the behavior of interest.

Part 0: Getting attention weights can make a model behave differently

A while ago, I was analyzing the attention patterns of a vision-language model when I noticed something strange: its accuracy on my benchmark dropped from about 70% to 20% after I enabled output_attentions=True. I hadn't changed anything else other than that one argument for output_attentions. How could observing the model change its behavior so much?

One warning message caught my eye:

`torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` does not support `output_attentions=True`. Falling back to eager attention. This warning can be removed using the argument `attn_implementation="eager"` when loading the model.

So, requesting attention weights changed the attention implementation. The model I was trying to inspect was no longer being executed in the same way as the model whose behavior interested me.

Motivated by the huge performance drop, I wanted to understand whether switching attention implementations really could change model outputs, how much floating-point precision mattered, and whether there was a way to recover attention weights without switching away from the original computation.

That also leads to a broader question for interpretability: how do we make sure that we are studying the computational artifact that actually exhibited the behavior of interest?

Part I: Same weights can produce different behavioral outputs under different attention implementations

Attention implementations are supposed to compute the same underlying operation. But mathematically equivalent doesn't always mean numerically identical: fused kernels may group and round floating-point operations differently. The practical question is whether these numerical differences can lead to different observed model behavior (i.e. generated text). In the meantime, small rounding errors that do not lead to a difference in behavior would be fine and should not be a big problem.

I compared three attention backends while holding everything else fixed:

  • Eager: Hugging Face attn_implementation="eager", which explicitly materializes attention weights.
  • SDPA: attn_implementation="sdpa", using PyTorch's regular scaled-dot-product-attention dispatch.
  • FA2: attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", using the external FlashAttention 2 package.

All continuations below use greedy decoding to make sure the process is deterministic. If two runs generate different token sequences, the difference cannot be attributed to random token sampling, and must be from the attention implementation.

The same input results in different continuations

We begin with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct in BF16, using the prompt "Describe the image." and a COCO image of a bakery counter.

The identical input image for all three BF16 generations: COCO val2017 image 226903. Prompt: “Describe the image.”

To see whether this was an isolated example, I ran the same prompt on 20 randomly sampled COCO images. The counts below shows whether the there exists any generated different token among the output sequences between each pair of backends:

Backend comparison Images with different continuations
Eager vs. SDPA 17/20
Eager vs. FA2 17/20
SDPA vs. FA2 15/20

15-17 out of 20 generations result in different output sequences across the three attention backends. While this does not necessarily mean they convey very different semantic information, it is already quite bothersome if we want to study some low-level/token-level mechanisms or predictions -- just by using another attention backend, the mechanism of interest may no longer be used.

Code: compare greedy text and next-token logits 
from urllib.request import urlopen

import torch
from PIL import Image
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
vlm = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="eager",
).to("cuda").eval()
image = Image.open(urlopen(
    "https://s3.amazonaws.com/images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000226903.jpg"
)).convert("RGB")
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "image", "image": image},
    {"type": "text", "text": "Describe the image."},
]}]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")


def compare_backends(model, inputs, decoder, backends):
    logits, texts = {}, {}
    for backend in backends:
        model.set_attn_implementation(backend)
        with torch.inference_mode():
            logits[backend] = model(**inputs, use_cache=False).logits[0, -1].cpu()
            tokens = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, num_beams=1,
                                    max_new_tokens=128)
        generated = tokens[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
        texts[backend] = decoder.decode(generated, skip_special_tokens=True)
    return logits, texts


backends = ["eager", "sdpa", "flash_attention_2"]
logits, texts = compare_backends(vlm, inputs, processor, backends)
for backend, text in texts.items():
    print(backend, text)

The differences are visible in next-token logits

Different continuations can amplify small numerical changes over many generation steps. To take a closer look at the upstream cause, here I compare next-token logits on the identical image-and-prompt prefix.

For every input, I calculate the root-mean-squared difference between each pair of backends' logits, then average this value over the 20 inputs:

\[ M_{ab}=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{i=1}^{20}\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal V|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal V}(z_{i,v}^{(a)}-z_{i,v}^{(b)})^2}. \]
Backend comparison (BF16) Mean next-token logit RMSE
Eager vs. SDPA 0.11302
Eager vs. FA2 0.11435
SDPA vs. FA2 0.087053

So the runs already have measurably different next-token scores on the same prefix, even before we compare their later continuations.

Another view: maximum absolute logit differences

For each input, I also compute the largest absolute difference over vocabulary entries, then average those per-input maximum values, to get a better sense of the magnitude of maximal differences.

Backend comparison (BF16) Mean per-image maximum absolute difference
Eager vs. SDPA 0.51472
Eager vs. FA2 0.54028
SDPA vs. FA2 0.42119
Code: compute the averaged pairwise logit matrix 
import torch


def pairwise_logit_differences(logits_by_input):
    # One [backend, vocabulary] tensor per identical input prefix.
    z = torch.stack(logits_by_input).double()  # [input, backend, vocabulary]
    difference = z[:, :, None, :] - z[:, None, :, :]
    rmse = difference.square().mean(-1).sqrt().mean(0)
    max_abs = difference.abs().amax(-1).mean(0)
    return rmse, max_abs


# Opening example only. For the 20-input average, pass 20 such tensors.
logits_by_input = [torch.stack([logits[b] for b in backends])]
rmse, max_abs = pairwise_logit_differences(logits_by_input)
print(rmse)
print(max_abs)

Precision makes a substantial difference

If the choice of attention backend matters because of numerical computation, what happens when we change the floating-point precision?

I repeat the Qwen3-VL comparison on the same 20 inputs, holding precision fixed within each backend comparison:

Precision Different sequences: eager vs. SDPA Mean next-token logit RMSE
BF16 17/20 0.11302
FP16 6/20 0.016291
FP32 0/20 0.000012276

The implementations agree much more closely at higher precision on these inputs. In FP32 especially, eager and SDPA generated identical token sequences across all 20 inputs, with a near zero logit RMSE difference. This pattern suggests that float number precision also plays an important role in determining model's behavior, as suggested in prior work (e.g. Qi et al., 2025).

However, since many models (such as the Qwen models) are trained in BF16 with flash attention and suggests inference to use the same setup, even if there is a better consistency across attention backends at FP32, switching to FP32 would cause a difference in behavior that is undesirable for carrying out interpretability analysis (see appendix for related comparisons).

Full FP16/FP32 comparisons, including FA2
Precision Backend comparison Different sequences Mean logit RMSE
FP16 Eager vs. SDPA 6/20 0.016291
FP16 Eager vs. FA2 4/20 0.018746
FP16 SDPA vs. FA2 6/20 0.014249
FP32 Eager vs. SDPA 0/20 0.000012276

FA2 was unavailable in FP32 in this setup since it does not support this precision.

Code: repeat the VLM comparison at FP16 and FP32 
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText

# Reuse inputs, processor and compare_backends from the first example.
for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.float32):
    methods = ["eager", "sdpa"]
    if dtype == torch.float16:
        methods.append("flash_attention_2")  # FA2 does not support FP32.
    precision_model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
        model_id, dtype=dtype, attn_implementation="eager",
    ).to("cuda").eval()
    z, text = compare_backends(precision_model, inputs, processor, methods)
    print(dtype, text)
    print(pairwise_logit_differences([torch.stack([z[b] for b in methods])])[0])
    del precision_model

Code: reproduce the two BF16 text-model controls 
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

# One prefix is shown; use continuation20.json for the 20-prefix average.
prefix = "Fifty years later, the small coastal town had become"
for checkpoint in ("Qwen/Qwen3-4B", "openai-community/gpt2"):
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
    lm = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        checkpoint, dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="eager",
    ).to("cuda").eval()
    text_inputs = tokenizer(prefix, add_special_tokens=False,
                            return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
    z, text = compare_backends(lm, text_inputs, tokenizer, backends)
    print(checkpoint, text)
    print(pairwise_logit_differences([torch.stack([z[b] for b in backends])])[0])
    del lm

The interpretability problem remains: if requesting attention weights causes a switch from SDPA or FA2 to eager, we may end up measuring internal patterns from a run that doesn't even generate the same sequence as the original. What then should we do to (1) access faithful intermediate computational variables and (2) not change the model's native computation graph?

Part II: Recovering attention from fused kernels

Part I exposed a practical problem: the attention implementation that produces the behavior we want to understand may not expose its attention weights. With optimized backends such as SDPA and FlashAttention, the full attention matrix is often never materialized as an accessible tensor. Asking for it through output_attentions=True can instead switch the model to eager attention—and, as we've seen, switching implementations can change the generated continuation.

Can we recover the attention weights of the original backend without switching to a different implementation?

This is in principle doable. We don't need the kernel to return its attention matrix. We can patch the values supplied to it and observe its output. By choosing the values carefully, we can leverage the existing blackbox attention kernel to reconstruct the attention weights. This idea was suggested in this PyTorch discussion. I'll walk through the intuition, explain how to use it for long sequences, and then test how accurately it recovers attention from real backends.

1. The trick: reconstructing attention weights with identity value matrices

The final step of a single attention head is:

\[ Z = AV. \]

Here, \(A\) is the attention matrix we want, \(V\) contains the value vectors, and \(Z\) is the attention output. An optimized kernel may give us \(Z\) without ever exposing \(A\).

Consider the following observation: if we set \(V\) to an identity matrix, the output becomes \(A\) itself, via \(AI=A\).

That gives us a way to reconstruct attention weights using the original kernel. We leave all other variables unchanged, and replace only the value vectors.

In practice, the value dimension is usually much smaller than the sequence length, so we can't fit the entire identity matrix into a single attention call. We can use partial identities: each call reveals a block of columns, and several calls recover the complete matrix.

Reading attention from its output. (A) Replacing the value vectors with a partial identity reveals the corresponding columns of the attention matrix. (B) Shifting the identity entries across successive passes recovers the remaining columns, which are concatenated.

For example, if a sequence has six key positions but each value vector has only two dimensions, each identity-value pass reveals two columns of attention. Three passes recover all six columns. More generally, a sequence with \(T_k\) key positions and value dimension \(d_v\) takes \(\lceil T_k/d_v\rceil\) passes.

The key part is that this doesn't require the fused kernel to produce a full attention matrix internally. We reconstruct it from the kernel's responses to carefully chosen values.

Code: a minimal example of identity-value recovery 
import torch

for length, head_dim in [(2, 4), (6, 2)]:
    # Toy attention weights: the fused kernel is represented here by A @ V.
    A = torch.softmax(
        torch.randn(length, length, dtype=torch.float64), dim=-1
    )
    blocks = []

    for offset in range(0, length, head_dim):
        width = min(head_dim, length - offset)
        V = torch.zeros(length, head_dim, dtype=A.dtype)
        V[offset:offset + width, :width] = torch.eye(
            width, dtype=A.dtype
        )
        Z = A @ V
        blocks.append(Z[:, :width])

    recovered = torch.cat(blocks, dim=-1)
    torch.testing.assert_close(recovered, A, atol=0, rtol=0)
    print((length, head_dim), recovered.shape)

2. Applying the trick to a real attention implementation

The mathematical idea is simple. To use it with a real transformer, we need access to the attention operation at the point where its values enter and its output leaves. We need to be able to replace intermediate value tensors and read intermediate outputs.

Using NNsight, we can do the following for a selected attention head on HF open-sourced models:

  1. Run the model with the desired setup, so that the queries and keys correspond to the computation we're studying.
  2. Repeat the attention computation with successive partial-identity value tensors, keeping the queries, keys, mask, and other attention settings fixed.
  3. Read each resulting attention output at the boundary before the output projection (o_proj), and concatenate the recovered blocks to construct the full attention matrix.

Through these steps, we get both the behavior of interest, and the attention weights reconstructed from the corresponding runs.

There is one practical detail when extracting many layers or heads: replacing values at an early layer can change the inputs to later layers. If we want attention weights from the original later-layer computation, we must keep its inputs fixed. We use a clean cache built from an unmodified execution and restore the original activation before continuing to collect later layer attention weights: this reduces the number of runs we needed to reconstruct attention weights across all layers.

Implementation detail: recovering many heads without contaminating later layers

Attention head output activation restoration. When multiple layers are inspected in a shared computation, the original attention output can be restored after each identity-value pass so that subsequent layers receive their original inputs.

In our implementation, we record the clean attention output, perform each identity-value pass, save its output for reconstruction, and restore the clean output at the input to o_proj.

3. How good is the recovery?

There is another caveat. The equation \(Z=AV\) holds exactly in principle, but an optimized GPU kernel computes in finite precision and can fuse or reorder operations. The recovered matrix is therefore best viewed as a numerical approximation to the attention weights relevant to that backend.

To evaluate that approximation, we ask the following question: can the recovered attention matrix reconstruct the attention output observed during the original forward pass?

We first recover a matrix \(A_{\mathrm{pred}}\) using partial identities. Then we multiply it by the original value vectors \(V_{\mathrm{real}}\), and compare the prediction with the clean attention output \(Z(V_{\mathrm{real}})\) from the original forward pass.

We measure their difference as relative reconstruction error: a smaller percentage means the recovered matrix more closely reproduces the native kernel's output.

Evaluation details: reconstruction error and controls
\[ \mathrm{Error}(\%)=100\,\frac{\left\|A_{\mathrm{pred}}V_{\mathrm{real}}-Z(V_{\mathrm{real}})\right\|_F}{\left\|Z(V_{\mathrm{real}})\right\|_F}. \]

Here, \(\|\cdot\|_F\) is the Frobenius norm. We compare against the output visible immediately before the attention output projection, using the native backend's own computation.

Inputs and head selection. Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct uses the same 20 COCO images with “Describe the image” as the previous experiments. Qwen3-4B and GPT-2 use the same 20 unfinished prose prefixes.

We select three decoder layers and three heads per layer. Both Qwen models use layers 0, 17, 35 and heads 0, 16, 31; GPT-2 uses layers 0, 5, 11 and heads 0, 6, 11. In total, we have 3 models x 3 layers x 3 heads x 3 backends x 20 inputs = 1,620 comparisons.

Measurement and precision. Using NNsight, we record the original values and the clean activation immediately before the attention output projection. Native attention and identity-value patching run in BF16. The evaluation product \(A_{\mathrm{pred}}V_{\mathrm{real}}\) is computed in float64 to limit additional evaluation error.

Across all 1,620 comparisons, reconstruction errors range from 0.086% to 0.297%, with a mean of 0.182%. These results show that the recovered matrices thus closely reproduce the attention outputs observed during the original forward pass.

4. How does backend-recovered attention compare with the eager-returned attention weights?

We could also obtain attention weights from eager and use them to analyze a model run under SDPA or FA2. Part I gives us a reason to be cautious: separate backend executions can differ even when the inputs are identical. In this section, we compare the error from using the extracted attention weights from a run's own backend to the error from using the eager-returned attention weights. For Qwen3-VL decoder attention under FA2, for example, the mean errors are 0.192% with FA2-recovered weights and 10.593% with eager-returned weights.

Attention-output reconstruction error (%) — lower is better

Model Target backend Recovered from target Eager returned
Qwen3-VL-4B Eager 0.160% 0.160%
Qwen3-VL-4B SDPA 0.192% 8.135%
Qwen3-VL-4B FA2 0.192% 10.593%
Qwen3-4B Eager 0.152% 0.152%
Qwen3-4B SDPA 0.196% 1.361%
Qwen3-4B FA2 0.197% 1.361%
GPT-2 Eager 0.155% 0.155%
GPT-2 SDPA 0.196% 0.825%
GPT-2 FA2 0.196% 0.816%

For both SDPA and FA2, using weights recovered from the target backend gives lower mean reconstruction error than using the eager-returned attention weights. This supports the use of backend-specific extraction when the goal is to explain the attention computation that actually ran.

5. Recovering attention in practice

I've packaged this approach as AttnRead so others can use it in their own research:

pip install attnread

Related issues reported online

Other users have encountered related problems when comparing or inspecting attention implementations:

  • Different logits on image inputs. A Qwen2.5-VL discussion, also reported in Transformers issue #39067, describes larger backend logit differences for image inputs than for text inputs.
  • Changed behavior while requesting attention weights. Transformers issue #35270 reports unexpected outputs when using eager attention to inspect a LLaVA model. It illustrates the practical concern that the attention-inspection configuration can affect the behavior being studied.
  • Fused attention does not normally expose the full pattern. PyTorch issue #119811 discusses this interpretability need and suggests probing with identity values.

Discussion

When we say we are interpreting a model, what exactly identifies that model? A checkpoint specifies its parameters, but those parameters can be executed through different computational implementations. As we've seen, changing the attention backend or floating-point precision can produce different greedy continuations, even when the model weights, inputs, and decoding settings remain fixed. In practice, a checkpoint alone does not fully specify the computational artifact whose behavior we are trying to explain.

This matters when our interpretability methods require modifying how the model is executed. Suppose a model exhibits some behavior under a fused attention backend, but requesting its attention weights silently switches the implementation to eager. The resulting attention patterns may come from an execution that behaves differently on the very input we're interested in. Even if the two executions produce similar outputs, we cannot simply assume that their internal computations are interchangeable.

Our approach to attention recovery illustrates one way forward: rather than changing the computation to make it easier to inspect, we can design our measurements around the computation we actually want to understand. By recovering attention weights directly from the original backend, and validating them against its native outputs, we can establish a closer connection between the quantities we extract and the computation that produced them.

Of course, not every numerical difference between implementations will matter for every interpretability question. Different token sequences do not necessarily imply different semantic behavior, and small numerical discrepancies need not invalidate an analysis. What matters is whether the measurements we obtain faithfully characterize the computation relevant to the phenomenon we're studying.

The broader lesson extends beyond attention visualization. Whenever an interpretability method changes the execution environment, numerical precision, or computation being inspected, we should ask whether those changes affect what we're trying to explain. Before explaining a model's behavior, we need to establish that we're interpreting the computation that produced it.
